title: In fallen man the first power remains, the second is lost and turned into its contrary
source_text: XXXIII. Quibus positis, affirmat in nobis per peccatum corruptis esse potentiam primam, sive principium materiale tam bene quam male agendi, sed amissam esse per peccatum Adami potentiam secundam, sive principium formale bene agendi, nec amissam modo, sed in contrariam potentiam conversam, ut ad id quod demum est bene agere secundum Deum, in omnibus nostris facultatibus moralibus insit universalis repugnantia, eo tenacior quod & ab ipso ortu insita est, & perpetua consuetudine, quasi altera natura, confirmata.
pass_a_gloss: XXXIII. Which things being laid down, he affirms that in us, corrupted through sin, there is the first power, or material principle of acting both well and ill, but that through the sin of Adam the second power, or formal principle of acting well, was lost, and not only lost, but turned into a contrary power, so that toward that which in the end is to act well according to God, there is in all our moral faculties a universal repugnance, the more tenacious because it is both implanted from our very birth, and confirmed by perpetual custom, as a second nature.
pass_b_english: On these premises he holds that in us, corrupted by sin, the first power remains, the material principle of acting either well or badly. The second power, the formal principle of acting well, was lost through Adam's sin.

It was not merely lost but changed into the opposite power. So all our moral faculties carry a universal resistance to the one thing that finally is acting well according to God, and it is all the more stubborn because it is ingrained from birth and reinforced by constant habit, like a second nature.

lemmas.latin: amissam esse per peccatum Adami potentiam secundam
lemmas.gloss: through the sin of Adam the second power was lost

choices.why: The Schools' distinction between a remote (merely capable) and a proximate (ready to act) power; kept as technical terms.
